title: Amos 3:9–15
context: The LORD summons the palaces of Ashdod and Egypt to witness the oppression in Samaria, where people hoard plunder and no longer know how to do right. An adversary will overrun the land, and only remnants will be rescued, like a shepherd recovering two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion. The LORD will visit the altars of Bethel and destroy the winter houses, summer houses, and houses of ivory. The identity of the adversary and some details of the imagery are held cautiously. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as judgment on injustice and corrupted worship.

verses.text: Proclaim in the palaces at Ashdod, and in the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, “Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see what unrest is in her, and what oppression is among them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos calls for a proclamation in the palaces of Ashdod and Egypt: assemble on Samaria’s mountains and see the unrest and oppression within. Arminian readers see foreign nations called to witness.

Even outsiders are summoned to judge Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The choice of Philistia and Egypt, former oppressors, sharpens the irony.

Reformed readers see God exposing Israel’s sin publicly. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God bringing Israel’s injustice into the open.

verses.text: “Indeed they don’t know to do right,” says the LORD, “Who hoard plunder and loot in their palaces.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Indeed they don’t know to do right,” describing those who hoard plunder and loot in their palaces.

Arminian readers see moral blindness produced by habitual injustice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The palaces become storehouses of goods gained by oppression.

Reformed readers see the corrupted conscience. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a sober diagnosis of wealth gained by violence and the loss of the ability to do right.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: “An adversary will overrun the land; and he will pull down your strongholds, and your fortresses will be plundered.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says an adversary will overrun the land, pull down the strongholds, and plunder the fortresses. Judgment answers plunder with plunder.

Arminian readers see consequences matching the sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
The adversary is not named; many readers think of Assyria, though the text leaves it open.

Reformed readers see God using nations as instruments of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s judgment on Samaria.

verses.text: The LORD says: “As the shepherd rescues out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued who sit in Samaria on the corner of a couch, and on the silken cushions of a bed.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that as a shepherd rescues from a lion’s mouth two legs or a piece of an ear, so the children of Israel in Samaria will be rescued. The rescue is minimal.

Arminian readers see judgment leaving little.
verses.reformedNotes:
A shepherd might bring remains as evidence that an animal was killed (compare Exodus 22:13). The image is ironic, pointing to near total loss.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: both traditions read this soberly.

verses.text: “Listen, and testify against the house of Jacob,” says the Lord GOD, the God of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD, the God of Armies, calls for testimony against the house of Jacob. A courtroom tone enters.

Arminian readers see God presenting his case so that the justice of his judgment is clear to all who hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
The call to “testify” may be addressed to the foreign witnesses of verse 9.

Reformed readers see God’s just accusation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a solemn charge against the house of Jacob, grounded in the injustice already described.

verses.text: “For in the day that I visit the transgressions of Israel on him, I will also visit the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar will be cut off, and fall to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the LORD punishes Israel, he will visit the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off and fall.

Arminian readers see judgment reaching corrupted worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Bethel was a royal sanctuary (compare 1 Kings 12:28–29 and Amos 7:13). Altar horns may have been seen as places of refuge, though their meaning here is debated.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: false worship offers no protection.

verses.text: I will strike the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory will perish, and the great houses will have an end,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will strike the winter house with the summer house, and houses of ivory and great houses will end. Wealth will be lost.

Arminian readers see luxury built on oppression judged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ahab’s “ivory house” is mentioned in 1 Kings 22:39; the ivory here may refer to inlaid decoration, though details are uncertain.

Reformed readers see pride humbled. Shared ground: both traditions read this soberly as judgment on wealth gained unjustly.
